Not!
NOT
interjection (Gen X slang)
The sentence-final Not! that reverses everything before it ("That was a great movie … NOT!") was used on Saturday Night Live by Steve Martin in the late 1970s and appears in scattered American speech earlier, but it became a national craze through the SNL "Wayne’s World" sketches (from 1989) and the film Wayne’s World (1992), starring Mike Myers and Dana Carvey. The underlying word is the ordinary English negative not.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

The Gen X Not! is a little machine for saying two things at once: a sincere-sounding statement, a pause, and then the punchline that cancels it. "I’d love to clean my room … NOT!" It is the grammar of irony, and irony was Gen X’s native tongue. The Christian observation is that God speaks the other way. "As God is true, our word toward you was not yea and nay. For the Son of God, Jesus Christ … was not yea and nay, but in him was yea. For all the promises of God in him are yea, and in him Amen" (2Co 1:18-20). There is no punchline in the gospel; nothing God has said will be reversed in the last beat. Our Lord asks His people to speak the same way: "let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay" (Mat 5:37). Proverbs warns about the man who deceives his neighbour and then says, "Am not I in sport?" (Pro 26:19) — the joke that was really a lie. The playful Not! between friends is not wicked; but a generation that learned to never quite mean what it said found it hard to say "I love you," "I was wrong," and "I believe" without reaching for the escape hatch. Christians are called to be people whose yes stays yes.

Webster 1828 Definition

Gen X sentence-final reversal ("Great idea … NOT!"), popularized by SNL’s "Wayne’s World" (1989–92); the grammar of irony, set against a God whose promises are all yea and amen in Christ (2Co 1:20).

NOT!, interj. (Gen X slang, late 1980s–early 1990s) Appended after a pause to reverse a preceding statement: "He’s a genius … NOT!"

Popularized by the SNL "Wayne’s World" sketches (1989 onward) and the film (1992); earlier SNL use by Steve Martin.

Kin to psyche! and just kidding: the statement offered and withdrawn in one breath.

Webster 1828: NOT, adv. [See Naught.] 1. A word that expresses negation, denial or refusal. …

Decode for parents: irony is a tool; a life built on it never quite commits — teach a yes that stays yes.

Key Scripture

2Co 1:18 — "But as God is true, our word toward you was not yea and nay."

2Co 1:19 — "For the Son of God, Jesus Christ, who was preached among you by us, even by me and Silvanus and Timotheus, was not yea and nay, but in him was yea."

2Co 1:20 — "For all the promises of God in him are yea, and in him Amen, unto the glory of God by us."

Mat 5:37 — "But let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay: for whatsoever is more than these cometh of evil."

Pro 26:19 — "So is the man that deceiveth his neighbour, and saith, Am not I in sport?"

Modern Corruption

Not! is the grammar of irony — the statement offered and withdrawn; God’s word in Christ is never yea and nay, and His people are called to a yes that stays yes.

expand to see more

The escape hatch. Irony protects the speaker: if the room laughs, he meant it as a joke; if the room agrees, he meant it. Gen X perfected the posture, and Not! was its catchphrase. The cost is that sincerity begins to feel naked and dangerous. Proverbs names the moral edge of it: the man who deceives and then says "Am not I in sport?" (Pro 26:19) uses the joke as cover.

The God without a punchline. Paul’s answer to the charge of fickleness was theological: because God is true, His word is not yea and nay, and in Christ every promise is yea and amen (2Co 1:18-20). The Christian’s speech is meant to image that. Humor is a gift; but a man must be able to say the important things straight, without the pause and the reversal.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Old English nawiht (nothing) → not; the sentence-final reversal Not! (Steve Martin, SNL, late 1970s; "Wayne’s World," 1989–92); Scripture: in Christ all the promises are yea (2Co 1:20).

expand to see more

Old English nawiht / noht — nothing → Middle English not

Late 1970s: Steve Martin uses the reversing Not! on Saturday Night Live

1989 onward: SNL "Wayne’s World" (Mike Myers, Dana Carvey) makes it a craze

1992 film Wayne’s World; the word becomes the emblem of Gen X irony

Biblical speech: yea, yea; nay, nay (Mat 5:37); God’s promises all yea in Christ (2Co 1:20)

Usage

""Oh yeah, algebra is my favorite … NOT!""

"The gospel has no "Not!" at the end; in Him was yea (2Co 1:19)."

"Let a joke be a joke, but let your yes be yes (Mat 5:37)."
